note: Literature in English round 3 (part A): twelve new unseen passages (six poems, three prose extracts, three drama extracts) with appreciation questions, plus stand-alone items on literary devices, figures of speech and poetic terms built around fresh example lines.

passages.title: Queue at the Borehole (unseen poem)
passages.text:
Before the cock has cleared its throat,
the jerrycans are already there,
yellow soldiers standing in a line
no general ever ordered.
The borehole coughs, spits, then sings,
and twenty women lean into its song.
Mama Nkechi guards her place like land;
a girl of six defends a bucket
taller than her patience.
When the handle sighs its last, dry sigh,
the queue does not disperse. It waits,
the way a village waits for rain,
the way the poor have always waited,
with jerrycans, with jokes, with God.

passages.title: Letter to a Brother in Toronto (unseen poem)
passages.text:
You write that the snow is kind this year,
that the cold has learned your name.
Here the sun still argues with the roof
and NEPA keeps its old promises: none.
Mama has framed your graduation photo
beside the calendar of a bank that closed.
She dusts you every Saturday.
Send the money when you can, she says,
and means: send yourself.
The mango you planted fruits without you;
we eat them and do not speak of it.
Come back, brother, or do not come back,
but write. The cold, you say, is kind.
Kindness was never what we lacked.

passages.title: Harvest of Rust (unseen poem)
passages.text:
The looms are quiet. Where thread ran
like rivers through a thousand fingers,
spiders spin the only cloth in town.
The gate that swallowed two thousand men
each dawn, and spat them out at dusk,
hangs from one hinge, a broken jaw.
Baba worked here. His hands still move
at night, feeding looms no longer there.
We harvest rust now, and a kind of rage
with no factory to go to in the morning.

passages.title: The Tree at Number Twelve (unseen poem)
passages.text:
The mango tree at Number Twelve is gone;
a wall of grey blocks stands in its place.
We climbed it when the school day was done
and dared the branches to a higher race.
Its shade held Baba Tailor's rented chair,
where gossip ripened faster than fruit,
and every child in Surulere knew there
was one ripe mango no one would dispute.
The landlord's son came back from overseas
with drawings and a chainsaw's steady hum;
the tree came down in pieces by degrees,
and nobody had told us it would come.
The wall is tidy, freshly painted, bare;
no fruit, no shade; nobody gathers there.

passages.title: Night Shift (unseen poem)
passages.text:
At 2 a.m. the ward forgets to breathe;
only the drip counts seconds on its beads.
Sister Ugo moves from bed to bed,
a lighthouse on soft shoes.
Bed Four is calling for a mother
dead these thirty years. She answers.
Bed Nine will not see morning; she knows,
and straightens his sheet as if he might.
Outside, the generator preaches
its one loud sermon to the dark.
At six she signs the register: no change.
Everything has changed. She goes home.

passages.title: Okada (unseen poem)
passages.text:
He wears the city on his back:
a nurse, a bag of rice, a coffin once,
three schoolchildren stacked like plates.
Between the buses and the gutters
he threads a needle nobody else can see.
The policeman at the bridge knows his name
and the price of forgetting it.
At night he counts notes soft as leaves,
sends half to a village that calls him
engineer, because he once was.

passages.title: First Day at St. Jude's (unseen prose)
passages.text: The gate of St. Jude's was taller than any gate I had seen, and it was painted the green of unripe pawpaw. My father carried my metal box on his head the way he carried yams from the farm, and I walked behind him with the bucket and the new mattress rolled under my arm, trying not to look like a boy who had never slept away from home. Senior students lounged on the steps of the dormitory like lizards on a warm wall. One of them, a tall boy with a torn collar, looked at my father's bare feet, then at my shoes, and smiled a smile I would learn to fear. 'JJC,' he said softly, as we passed. I did not know then what it meant. I know now that it meant everything: that I was new, that I was raw, that I would be broken and remade in this place, and that my father, who had sold two goats to bring me here, would never see any of it.

passages.title: The Road (unseen prose)
passages.text: The elders met under the iroko as they had always met, though the iroko was now only a stump and a memory of shade. Chief Okoro spoke first, because he always spoke first, and said the government road must pass through the eastern farms. He did not mention that the eastern farms belonged to the Nwosu family, with whom he had quarrelled for thirty years. Pa Nwosu, who knew exactly what was not being mentioned, replied that the western route was shorter, cheaper and kinder to the stream; he did not mention that the western route would pass through Chief Okoro's cashew plantation. The young surveyor from the ministry, who understood none of this, wrote 'community undecided' in his notebook and thought about his lunch. Above them, the sky, which had watched such meetings for a hundred years, prepared, without much interest, to rain.

passages.title: The Interview (unseen prose)
passages.text: Ngozi had ironed the blouse twice. It did not matter; by the time the bus reached Marina the blouse had forgotten the iron entirely. Seventeen of them sat in the corridor, seventeen first-class brains in second-hand shoes, each pretending not to count the others. The door opened every twenty minutes and swallowed one. Nobody came out that way. When her turn came, the man behind the desk did not look up from her file. 'Ngozi Okafor. Second class upper. Who do you know here?' She said she knew her subject. He smiled at the file, as if the file had made a joke. 'Everybody knows their subject, my dear.' Outside, afterwards, the sun was where she had left it, and she stood on the steps a long time, doing arithmetic that would not come out.

passages.title: Contract (extract from an unseen play)
passages.text:
ALHAJI SANI: (spreading a drawing across the desk) Six classrooms, Madam. Roofing, painting, everything. Finished before the rains.
MRS. BELLO: (not touching the drawing) The last contractor also said 'before the rains'. The rains came. The roof did not.
ALHAJI SANI: (laughing) That one was not a professional. Me, I have done work for the Ministry itself. Ask anybody.
MR. OKON: (aside, to the audience) I have asked. Everybody says the same thing: ask somebody else.
MRS. BELLO: And your price?
ALHAJI SANI: Twelve million. (pause) For the school, ten. (lower) And for Madam personally, there is always something for the goodwill.
MRS. BELLO: (rising) Mr. Okon, please show Alhaji the gate. And measure it; we may need a new one that closes faster.
(ALHAJI SANI gathers his drawing. At the door he turns.)
ALHAJI SANI: Madam, in this country, the one who refuses eats last.
MRS. BELLO: Then I will eat last, Alhaji. But I will eat with my own spoon.

passages.title: The Will (extract from an unseen play)
passages.text:
(A sitting room. A framed photograph of an old man hangs slightly crooked. UCHE, the elder brother, in a suit, checks his watch. OBI, the younger, in slippers, is arranging kola nuts on a tray.)
UCHE: The lawyer will be here at ten. Let us be sensible. The house in Enugu is mine; I am the first son. You take the farm.
OBI: The farm that Papa said was 'for whoever stays'. I stayed, Uche. Eleven years. You sent money and photographs.
UCHE: Money that built the very room you are standing in.
OBI: (quietly) And who stood in it when he could no longer stand?
(UCHE straightens the photograph. It tilts back.)
UCHE: We are not going to quarrel in front of a stranger.
OBI: No. We will quarrel in front of Papa. (He gestures at the photograph.) He is used to it.
(The doorbell rings. Neither moves.)

passages.title: From the Diary of a Trainee Teacher (unseen prose)
passages.text:
Monday. Forty-seven pupils, one chalk, no duster. I used my handkerchief. The headmaster says the chalk allocation 'finished' in February. It is October.
Tuesday. A girl named Halima solved the fraction problem before I had finished writing it. She hides her cleverness the way other children hide sweets. I must find out why.
Wednesday. Found out why. Her mother came to withdraw her; there is a husband waiting in the next village. I said the law. The mother said the rent. We were speaking two languages.
Thursday. The headmaster said, 'Mr Tunde, you are new. Do not carry what you cannot lift.' I said nothing. My handkerchief is white with chalk and I have started to think it is a flag.
Friday. Halima came to school. Her mother did not. I do not know what this means. I taught fractions again, slowly, as if speed were the enemy, and she solved everything, and I did not, for once, ask why.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: In 'Queue at the Borehole', the 'yellow soldiers standing in a line' are
questions.A: the children sent to fetch water at dawn
questions.B: the jerrycans placed in a queue by the women
questions.C: the women waiting their turn at the borehole
questions.D: the soldiers posted to guard the borehole
questions.explanation: The jerrycans, yellow and lined up before dawn, are pictured as soldiers on parade - a metaphor.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: 'The borehole coughs, spits, then sings' is an example of
questions.explanation: Coughing, spitting and singing are human actions given to the borehole as it starts to flow.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: The phrase 'no general ever ordered' suggests that the queue is
questions.A: an official arrangement enforced by the water board
questions.B: controlled strictly by the village head every morning
questions.C: made up of retired soldiers and their families
questions.D: a discipline created by need rather than by any authority
questions.explanation: The orderly line forms on its own; scarcity, not a commander, produces the discipline.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: 'Mama Nkechi guards her place like land' is a
questions.explanation: The comparison is made explicitly with 'like', so the device is a simile.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: The repetition of 'the way ... waits' and 'the way ... waited' in the closing lines is an example of
questions.explanation: Successive clauses begin with the same words ('the way'), which is anaphora.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: The tone of the final line, 'with jerrycans, with jokes, with God', is best described as
questions.A: open mockery of the women's religious faith
questions.B: bitter contempt for the laziness of the villagers
questions.C: cold indifference to the suffering described
questions.D: wry admiration for the endurance of the poor
questions.explanation: The poet notes humour and faith alongside the jerrycans, admiring the people's resilience with gentle irony.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: The poem is mainly concerned with
questions.A: the bravery of soldiers who protect village water supplies
questions.B: the patient endurance of ordinary people in the face of scarcity
questions.C: the beauty of the countryside at the break of day
questions.D: the conflict between Mama Nkechi and a little girl
questions.explanation: The queue, the failed handle and the waiting 'the way the poor have always waited' point to endurance under hardship.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: 'a bucket taller than her patience' suggests that the girl
questions.A: is more patient than any of the women around her
questions.B: has brought the biggest bucket in the whole queue
questions.C: is very small and is quickly losing patience with the long wait
questions.D: has been asked to carry water for the entire village
questions.explanation: The bucket dwarfs the six-year-old, and the comparison with her patience shows that her patience is short.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: In 'Letter to a Brother in Toronto', 'the cold has learned your name' suggests that the brother
questions.A: is unknown and lonely in the city he lives in
questions.B: is suffering badly from the Canadian winter
questions.C: has changed his name since arriving in Toronto
questions.D: has become settled and familiar in his new country
questions.explanation: The cold 'learning' his name is a personification implying that he now belongs there.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: 'NEPA keeps its old promises: none' is an example of
questions.explanation: The line pretends to praise NEPA for keeping promises, then reveals that it keeps none - verbal irony.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: 'She dusts you every Saturday' means that Mama
questions.A: sweeps his old room every Saturday morning
questions.B: scolds him on the telephone every weekend
questions.C: cleans his framed photograph as if she were tending him
questions.D: washes the clothes he left behind at home
questions.explanation: The photograph stands for the brother; dusting 'you' shows how she keeps him present.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: 'Send the money when you can, she says, and means: send yourself' reveals that Mama
questions.A: does not believe her son has any money to send
questions.B: cares more about money than about her son
questions.C: wants her son to stop sending money altogether
questions.D: hides her longing for her son behind practical requests
questions.explanation: What she says (money) and what she means (his return) differ; her real wish is for him.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: 'The mango you planted fruits without you' most likely symbolises
questions.A: the wealth the brother has made abroad
questions.B: life at home continuing in the brother's absence
questions.C: the family's anger at the brother's laziness
questions.D: the failure of the brother's plans in Toronto
questions.explanation: What he planted bears fruit he does not share - a symbol of home moving on without him.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: The speaker's attitude to the brother is best described as
questions.explanation: 'Come back, brother, or do not come back, but write' mixes affection with quiet rebuke.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: The last line, 'Kindness was never what we lacked', implies that
questions.A: Canada is a kinder country than Nigeria
questions.B: the family has always been unkind to the brother
questions.C: the brother left home because nobody was kind to him
questions.D: what the family lacked was opportunity, not human warmth
questions.explanation: The brother praises the kind cold; the speaker answers that kindness was plentiful at home - it was other things they lacked.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: The poem is written in the form of
questions.A: a sonnet with a final couplet
questions.B: a verse letter in free verse
questions.D: a dramatic monologue in blank verse
questions.explanation: It addresses the brother directly as a letter, without regular rhyme or metre.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: In 'Harvest of Rust', 'spiders spin the only cloth in town' is effective because it
questions.A: praises the skill of the spiders compared with the workers
questions.B: shows that the town has found a new source of income
questions.C: contrasts the factory's former weaving with the desolation of the present
questions.D: suggests that the factory will soon reopen
questions.explanation: Where looms once wove cloth, only cobwebs are 'woven' now - an ironic image of decline.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: The gate is compared to 'a broken jaw' by means of
questions.explanation: The gate is directly called a broken jaw, without 'like' or 'as', so the device is metaphor.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: 'The gate that swallowed two thousand men each dawn, and spat them out at dusk' presents the factory as
questions.A: a generous provider that fed the whole town
questions.B: a living creature that consumed the workers' days
questions.C: a prison from which nobody ever escaped
questions.D: a temple where the workers came to worship
questions.explanation: Swallowing and spitting are actions of a living thing - personification of the factory's daily routine.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: Baba's hands moving at night 'feeding looms no longer there' suggest that he
questions.A: is teaching his children how to weave
questions.B: has found night work at another factory
questions.C: cannot let go of the work that defined his life
questions.D: still goes to the factory every evening
questions.explanation: Even in sleep his hands repeat the old motions; the loss haunts him.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: The title 'Harvest of Rust' is ironic because
questions.A: the workers were paid in crops rather than money
questions.B: rust cannot be harvested by farmers
questions.C: the poem is set in a factory rather than on a farm
questions.D: a harvest suggests plenty while rust suggests decay
questions.explanation: The word 'harvest' promises reward; what is reaped is rust - the irony sums up the poem.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: 'a kind of rage with no factory to go to in the morning' suggests that
questions.A: the workers are too tired to be angry any more
questions.B: the anger of the unemployed has no outlet or direction
questions.C: the factory owners fear the workers' revenge
questions.D: the town has decided to build a new factory
questions.explanation: Like the workers, the rage has nowhere to go; it is idle and aimless.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: The dominant mood of 'Harvest of Rust' is one of
questions.explanation: Silent looms, a broken gate, rust and rage create a bleak, bitter mood.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: 'The Tree at Number Twelve' is, in form, a
questions.explanation: Fourteen lines in three quatrains and a closing couplet, rhyming abab cdcd efef gg.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: The rhyme scheme of the first four lines of 'The Tree at Number Twelve' is
questions.explanation: gone/done and place/race rhyme alternately: abab.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: 'where gossip ripened faster than fruit' uses
questions.explanation: Gossip is said to ripen like fruit without 'like' or 'as' - a metaphor.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: The mango tree in the poem functions mainly as a symbol of
questions.B: the wealth of the landlord's family
questions.explanation: Children, the tailor and gossip all gathered under it; its loss ends that common life.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: The landlord's son 'with drawings and a chainsaw's steady hum' represents
questions.A: a skilled craftsman restoring the compound
questions.B: a modernising generation indifferent to what the tree meant
questions.C: the return of prosperity to the neighbourhood
questions.D: the children who once climbed the tree
questions.explanation: He arrives from overseas with plans and destroys the tree without consulting anyone.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: The final couplet is effective because it
questions.A: shows that the children have found a new tree to climb
questions.B: explains why the landlord's son wanted the tree removed
questions.C: sets the neatness of the wall against the lifelessness that replaced the tree
questions.D: describes the fruit that the new wall now provides
questions.explanation: 'Tidy, freshly painted, bare' is answered by 'no fruit, no shade; nobody gathers there'.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: 'and nobody had told us it would come' conveys a feeling of
questions.A: excitement at the arrival of the chainsaw
questions.B: relief that the dangerous tree was finally removed
questions.C: gratitude to the landlord for the surprise
questions.D: helpless exclusion from a decision that affected the children
questions.explanation: The children were neither consulted nor warned; the line records their powerlessness.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: In the poem, 'by degrees' means
questions.explanation: The tree came down 'in pieces by degrees', that is, little by little.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: In 'Night Shift', 'the ward forgets to breathe' is an example of
questions.explanation: The ward is given the human capacity to breathe and forget.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: Sister Ugo is called 'a lighthouse on soft shoes' because she
questions.A: warns the patients loudly whenever danger comes
questions.B: is tall and can be seen from every bed in the ward
questions.C: carries a torch as she walks around at night
questions.D: is a steady source of comfort moving quietly among the patients
questions.explanation: A lighthouse guides and reassures; 'soft shoes' adds her quiet, unobtrusive care.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: Sister Ugo's response to the patient calling for a mother 'dead these thirty years' shows that she is
questions.A: confused about who the patient is calling
questions.C: impatient with the confused old patient
questions.D: the patient's daughter in real life
questions.explanation: 'She answers' - she meets the patient's need instead of pointing out his error.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: 'and straightens his sheet as if he might' reveals the nurse's
questions.A: carelessness about the condition of the patient
questions.B: belief that the patient will recover by morning
questions.C: tenderness in preserving the dignity of a dying man
questions.D: fear of being blamed for the patient's death
questions.explanation: She knows Bed Nine will die, yet treats him as though he had a future - an act of gentle respect.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: Describing the generator's noise as 'its one loud sermon to the dark' suggests that the sound is
questions.explanation: A single sermon repeated loudly all night conveys a droning, relentless noise.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: The contrast between 'no change' in the register and 'Everything has changed' is an example of
questions.explanation: The official record says nothing happened, while the truth is that a man died - situational irony.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: The poem's attitude towards Sister Ugo is one of
questions.explanation: Her steadiness, compassion and dignity are presented with restrained respect.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: In 'Okada', 'He wears the city on his back' means that the rider
questions.A: owns a large part of the city's property
questions.B: is dressed in clothes bought in the city
questions.C: has a map of the city printed on his shirt
questions.D: carries all kinds of people and loads for the city
questions.explanation: The following lines list his passengers and loads; the city literally rides on his back.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: 'three schoolchildren stacked like plates' is an example of
questions.explanation: The children are compared to stacked plates using 'like' - a simile.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: 'he threads a needle nobody else can see' suggests that the rider
questions.A: cannot see well and rides dangerously
questions.B: repairs clothes when he is not riding
questions.C: weaves skilfully through gaps in the traffic
questions.D: follows a route marked only on his map
questions.explanation: Threading an invisible needle pictures his skill in finding narrow paths between vehicles.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: 'the price of forgetting it' refers to
questions.A: the fare the rider charges his passengers
questions.B: the fine for riding without a licence
questions.C: the cost of repairing the motorcycle
questions.D: the bribe the policeman collects to let him pass
questions.explanation: The policeman 'knows his name' and the price of forgetting it - money paid to be left alone.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: 'engineer, because he once was' implies that the rider
questions.A: repairs motorcycles for the other riders in the village
questions.B: is a trained engineer forced by unemployment into riding okada
questions.C: lied to his village about his profession
questions.D: hopes to study engineering one day
questions.explanation: The village still calls him by the profession he trained for but can no longer practise.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: The poem's attitude to the okada rider is one of
questions.explanation: His skill, burdens and sacrifice for his village are presented with sympathy.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: 'notes soft as leaves' suggests that the money is
questions.A: green in colour like new leaves
questions.C: made of leaves rather than paper
questions.D: worn and fragile from passing through many hands
questions.explanation: Old notes become soft like fallen leaves; the simile also hints at how little they are worth.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: In 'First Day at St. Jude's', the story is told by
questions.A: the father of the new student
questions.B: an adult recalling his own first day at school
questions.C: a senior student watching the newcomers
questions.D: an outside narrator who knows all the characters
questions.explanation: 'I did not know then ... I know now' shows a first-person narrator looking back on his childhood.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: 'the green of unripe pawpaw' is an example of
questions.explanation: The phrase appeals to the sense of sight by describing an exact shade of green.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: 'Senior students lounged on the steps ... like lizards on a warm wall' is a simile that suggests the seniors are
questions.explanation: Lizards bask lazily but watch for movement; the seniors idle while sizing up the new boy.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: The senior's smile, which the narrator 'would learn to fear', is an example of
questions.explanation: It hints at the bullying to come, which the narrator will experience later.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: The contrast between the father's bare feet and the boy's shoes suggests
questions.A: that the boy is ashamed of his father's appearance
questions.B: the father's refusal to buy shoes for himself
questions.C: the father's sacrifice so that his son may have a better life
questions.D: that the school required all visitors to be barefoot
questions.explanation: The father goes without so that the boy is properly equipped; he even sold two goats for the fees.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: 'that I would be broken and remade in this place' suggests that the boarding school
questions.A: taught him a trade in pottery and carpentry
questions.B: was demolished and rebuilt during his time there
questions.C: expelled him and later readmitted him
questions.D: transformed the narrator through harsh experience
questions.explanation: 'Broken and remade' is a metaphor for the painful reshaping of his character.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: In the passage, the word 'JJC' functions as
questions.A: the name of the tall senior with the torn collar
questions.B: a label that marks the narrator as a raw newcomer
questions.C: the motto of St. Jude's written on the gate
questions.D: a greeting that the seniors gave to all visitors
questions.explanation: The narrator explains that it meant he was 'new' and 'raw' - an outsider's tag.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: The closing words 'would never see any of it' suggest that the father
questions.A: refused ever to visit his son at St. Jude's
questions.B: went blind soon after leaving the school
questions.C: remained shut out of the world his sacrifice had opened for his son
questions.D: was forbidden by the seniors to enter the school
questions.explanation: Having paid so much, the father would have no share in the life the school gave the boy.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: In 'The Road', the narrator
questions.A: reports only what could be seen and heard
questions.B: is Chief Okoro speaking for himself
questions.C: is the young surveyor telling his own story
questions.D: knows and reports the private thoughts of several characters
questions.explanation: The narrator tells us what each man 'did not mention' and what the surveyor thought - an omniscient narrator.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Appreciation
questions.q: 'the iroko was now only a stump and a memory of shade' suggests that
questions.A: the elders have planted a new iroko tree
questions.B: the traditions of the community have decayed

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: A stanza of eight lines is called
questions.explanation: An octave (or octet) has eight lines, as in the first part of a Petrarchan sonnet.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: Four lines of a poem end with the words 'day', 'night', 'play' and 'light'. The rhyme scheme is
questions.explanation: day/play rhyme (a) and night/light rhyme (b), alternating: abab.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: The voice that speaks in a poem, which need not be the poet's own, is called the
questions.explanation: The persona is the assumed speaker or 'mask' through which a poet speaks.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: A writer's choice of words, whether formal, colloquial or technical, is known as
questions.explanation: Diction refers to the selection of words in a literary work.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: 'The clash and clatter of cracked crockery' uses harsh, jarring sounds. This effect is called
questions.explanation: Cacophony is the deliberate use of harsh, discordant sounds.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: Lines in which soft, flowing sounds produce a pleasing musical effect, such as 'the murmuring of innumerable bees', illustrate
questions.explanation: Euphony is the use of pleasant, harmonious sounds.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: 'Slowly through the village walked the old priest' reverses the normal order of words. This device is
questions.explanation: Inversion (anastrophe) changes the usual subject-verb-object order for emphasis or rhythm.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: 'We had rice and beans and plantain and stew and still we were hungry' uses many conjunctions. This device is
questions.explanation: Polysyndeton is the deliberate repetition of conjunctions.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: 'He ran, stumbled, rose, ran again' omits conjunctions between the verbs. This device is
questions.explanation: Asyndeton leaves out conjunctions to quicken the pace.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: 'The silent snake slid softly across the stones' repeats the hissing /s/ sound. This effect is called
questions.explanation: Sibilance is the repetition of /s/ or /sh/ sounds, here imitating the snake's hiss.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: 'Time is a thief that leaves no fingerprints' is an example of
questions.explanation: Time is identified directly with a thief - an implied comparison.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: 'She is as stubborn as a locked gate' is an example of
questions.explanation: The comparison uses 'as ... as', making it a simile.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: 'Death, you have taken my mother; now leave my children alone' addresses death directly. The device is
questions.explanation: Speaking to an absent or abstract thing as if present is apostrophe (here also personification).

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: 'Our neighbour finally answered the last call' is a gentle way of saying that he died. This is
questions.explanation: A mild expression replaces a blunt reference to death.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: A poet writes, 'The sun crept out, apologetic, after the storm.' The word 'apologetic' is an example of
questions.explanation: The sun is given a human attitude - being apologetic.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: The main effect of a refrain in a poem or song is to
questions.A: emphasise a key idea and give the poem a musical structure
questions.B: introduce a new character in each stanza
questions.C: conceal the meaning of the poem from the reader
questions.D: shorten the poem so that it can be memorised
questions.explanation: Repetition at regular intervals stresses the central idea and creates rhythm.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: In the line 'The wind wept with the widow', the wind is made to share human grief. This device is called
questions.explanation: Pathetic fallacy attributes human emotions to nature, usually to reflect a character's feelings.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: 'Cruel kindness' and 'living death' are examples of
questions.explanation: Each phrase joins two contradictory words.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: In 'Nigeria won the match', the name of the country stands for its football team. The device is
questions.explanation: The country is named for the team closely associated with it - metonymy.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: 'The road ahead is dark, and the bridge is broken' said of a nation's future is an example of
questions.explanation: The nation's future is pictured as a journey along a road, without 'like' or 'as'.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: The line 'Ask the traffic. Ask the tray. Ask the silence at home.' relies chiefly on
questions.explanation: The repeated 'Ask the ...' gives the line its insistent force.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: A poet describes a corrupt official as 'this honourable thief'. The phrase is an example of
questions.explanation: 'Honourable' and 'thief' contradict each other and expose the man's hypocrisy.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: 'The market was a river of heads' is an example of
questions.explanation: The crowd is called a river directly; the comparison is implied.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: 'Justice is blind, but in this town she also seems deaf' plays on the traditional image of justice. The device is chiefly
questions.explanation: The remark mocks the failure of justice by extending a familiar image.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: A speaker says, 'I could sleep for a year.' This is
questions.explanation: The desire for sleep is exaggerated beyond possibility.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: The device in 'The pot called the kettle black' when used to describe a hypocrite is
questions.explanation: The expression is a proverbial saying whose meaning is not literal.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: The expression 'as brave as a lion' is a
questions.explanation: It compares using 'as ... as'.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: The general term for language that appeals to the senses - sight, sound, smell, taste and touch - is
questions.explanation: Imagery is descriptive language that creates sensory impressions.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: A poet calls the senators 'our tireless servants, resting in Dubai'. The tone of the line is
questions.explanation: The praise is mock praise; 'resting in Dubai' undercuts 'tireless servants' - the tone is sarcastic.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: The emotional atmosphere that a poem creates in the reader is its
questions.explanation: Mood is the feeling evoked in the reader, distinct from the writer's tone.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.topic: Literary Devices and Figures of Speech
questions.q: 'Sweet are the uses of adversity' is a memorable, compressed statement of a truth. Such a statement is
questions.explanation: An aphorism (or maxim) is a brief, pointed statement of a general truth.
